{{short description|American economist and statistician (1912-2012)}}
{{Distinguish|text=[[Margaret P. Martin]], a coeval American statistician}}
'''Margaret E. Martin''' (May 6, 1912 – May 16, 2012) was an economist and statistician at the U.S. [[Bureau of the Budget]] from 1942 to 1973.  She was influential in the development of U.S. economic statistics and became president of the [[American Statistical Association]].<ref name=washpost>Matt Schudel. {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20140319164057/http://articles.washingtonpost.com/2012-06-30/local/35460722_1_statistician-management-and-budget-labor-statistics|title="Margaret E. Martin, statistician"}}. Obituary in ''[[Washington Post]]'' June 30, 2012.</ref>

==Early life==
Margaret Elizabeth Martin was the first child born to Harry Martin, a teacher, and Frances Martin in New York in 1912. Her younger siblings were Jane, Eleanor and Robert.<ref name=washpost /><ref>1930 Federal Census. Yonkers, Westchester, New York. United States of America, Bureau of the Census. Fifteenth Census of the United States, 1930. Washington, D.C.: National Archives and Records Administration, 1930.</ref> As an elementary student, her teachers included noted economist [[Clara Eliot]].<ref name=leader/>

==Education==
In 1933, Martin received a bachelor's degree in economics from [[Barnard College]], and went on to earn an MA and PhD in economics from [[Columbia University]].<ref name=leader>[http://magazine.amstat.org/blog/2011/09/01/margaretmartin/ Margaret Martin: A Leader in the Federal Statistical System]. ''Amstat News''. 2011-09-01.</ref>

==Career==
Martin worked for the Division of Statistical Standards of the Bureau of the Budget beginning in 1942. The [[Current Population Survey]], which has been the primary source of labor statistics within the country, was developed by Martin and others. The survey is produced by the [[United States Census Bureau]] and the U.S. [[Bureau of Labor Statistics]] now.<ref name=washpost />

From 1973 to 1978 Martin was the first executive director of the Committee on National Statistics (CNSTAT) created by the [[United States National Research Council]].<ref name=amstat>[http://www.amstat.org/sections/srms/Proceedings/papers/1982_034.pdf Discussion - Margaret E. Martin, Committee on National Statistics.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304075724/http://www.amstat.org/sections/srms/Proceedings/papers/1982_034.pdf |date=2016-03-04 }} 1982. American Statistics Association, Online Proceedings of the Survey Research Methods Section.</ref>

==Recognition==
She was elected a [[Fellow of the American Statistical Association]] in 1961<ref>[http://www.amstat.org/awards/fellowslist.cfm List of ASA Fellows] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160616161612/http://www.amstat.org/awards/fellowslist.cfm |date=2016-06-16 }}, retrieved 2016-07-20.</ref> and became president in 1980.<ref name=washpost/> In 1989 the Association awarded her the [[American Statistical Association Founders Award|Founders Award]].<ref name=amstat/>

She was elected to the [[International Statistical Institute]] in 1973.<ref>{{citation|url=https://www.isi-web.org/index.php/about-isi/who-is-isi/members/in-memoriam|title=In memoriam|publisher=International Statistical Institute|accessdate=2017-11-21|archive-date=2017-12-01|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201042204/https://www.isi-web.org/index.php/about-isi/who-is-isi/members/in-memoriam|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Death==
Martin died May 16, 2012, of pneumonia and congestive heart failure at [[Suburban Hospital]] in [[Bethesda, Maryland]]. One of her sisters was alive at the time of her death.<ref name=washpost />
